extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, administrative lawyers, rulemaking practitioners, and members of the public who participate in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for federal administrative rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act, including procedural requirements for notices, comments, judicial review standards, information-collection approvals, and related executive-branch processes. Covers both substantive doctrines (e.g., Chevron/Loper Bright, Major Questions) and procedural requirements (e.g., NPRM, ICR, RFA, NEPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference (IBR) approval requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Act (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(1)) requires each agency to obtain the approval of the Director of the Office of the Federal Register for each document it wishes to incorporate by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations governing this approval are set out in Part 51 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations; advent of e-rulemaking affected incorporation of copyrighted voluntary industry standards; ACUS Recommendation 2011-5, OFR 2014 regulation update, and IBR Handbook (2016) provide further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent regulatory agency attributes and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent regulatory agencies are multi-member boards/commissions (e.g., FCC, FTC, NLRB, SEC) established by Congress to have some independence from the President; statutory attributes vary but often limit removal and partisan appointment control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although subject to the APA, independent agencies differ in that most Presidential Executive Orders do not apply (so they need not submit rules to OIRA under E.O. 12866), they are exempt from the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, and under the Paperwork Reduction Act they can, by majority vote, override an OMB/I OIRA rejection of an information collection request (44 U.S.C § 3502(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal rulemaking under APA Section 553 involves: (1) publishing a proposed rule in the Federal Register; (2) inviting public comment; (3) considering the public comment; and (4) publishing a final rule in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is intended to be a legislative-like process open to any 'interested person.' Much informal rulemaking is now e-rulemaking; paper comments still accepted. Other statutes and executive orders may add requirements that make the process more formalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to hold hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, an agency has discretion whether to hold an oral hearing unless its statute requires hearings in certain matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency holds a hearing it sets ground rules; hearings may range from informal (public statements for the record) to formal (sworn witnesses, cross-examination). See Hybrid Rulemaking where statutory requirements may mandate hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking exceptions to notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some types of rules are exempt from notice-and-comment procedures under Section 553 and other statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim final rules, interpretive rules, and other exceptions (discussed elsewhere on the page) may allow agencies to skip NPRM; each exception has doctrinal limits and case law governing its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) approval and content
rubrics_metrics.description: An ICR is a request to OMB/OIRA for approval of a 'collection of information' under the Paperwork Reduction Act; it must be approved before the collection begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICR documents must describe reporting/recordkeeping/survey requirements, justify the collection, and estimate cost and time for public response; agencies submit ICRs to OIRA via ROCIS; independent agencies can override OIRA rejections by majority vote (rarely exercised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rule / 'final rule with request for comments' and good-cause standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies sometimes issue a final rule and invite post-promulgation comments, using the 'good cause' exception to skip prior NPRM when notice would be 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique is not mentioned in the APA and is more accurately called 'Final Rule with Request for Comments' rather than 'Interim Final Rule.' It is often used when a statute requires quick agency action; originally coined by FAA. Labeling as 'interim' may be misleading if no termination date is specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rules and notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretive rule explains an agency's own regulation or the meaning of a statute it administers; APA permits agencies to issue interpretive rules without notice-and-comment (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Assoc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may sometimes add new content under the guise of interpretation, which can be challenged and potentially invalidated if it effectively imposes new requirements without notice-and-comment (e.g., Hoctor v. USDA). Each guidance or interpretive document must be examined individually to determine its true nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review grounds for agency rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts evaluate challenges to agency rules on three basic grounds: (1) agency lacked authority; (2) agency failed to follow proper procedure; (3) insufficient evidence supported the agency's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For informal rulemaking courts use the 'arbitrary or capricious' standard; for formal rulemaking or certain hybrid statutes they look for 'substantial evidence.' If procedural or substantive failures are found, courts normally vacate and remand the rule. Vermont Yankee limits courts from imposing extra procedures beyond statutory mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth test for adequacy of notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule must 'logically grow out of the terms of the proposed rule' so that commenters had adequate notice of the changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If final rule provisions are not a logical outgrowth, courts may require a new round of notice and comment. The Supreme Court adopted this test in Long Island Care at Home, Ltd. v. Coke (2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loper Bright Doctrine (Chevron overturned and Skidmore applied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) rejected Chevron deference; courts must use their own judgment to decide statutory ambiguities and should apply Skidmore deference to consider agency expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Loper Bright, courts no longer defer under Chevron but should consider agency 'body of experience and informed judgment' (Skidmore) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Questions Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The Major Questions Doctrine presumes Congress does not delegate authority over issues of great economic and political significance unless it provides clear authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have applied this doctrine in high-profile cases (e.g., West Virginia v. EPA, Ala. Ass’n of Realtors v. HHS, Biden v. Nebraska). The doctrine has influenced courts' willingness to cabin agency authority even prior to Chevron's overruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA environmental impact statement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPA requires federal agencies to include a detailed environmental impact statement (EIS) in every proposal for a major federal action significantly affecting the human environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EIS must address subjects and substantive criteria in NEPA; CEQ issued implementing regulations (40 CFR parts 1500–1508) and agencies should have supplementary regulations for assessing the need for an EIS and obtaining comments. (Page notes CEQ regulatory developments and guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated rulemaking (reg-neg) procedures and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiated rulemaking assembles representatives of affected stakeholders (with a convenor/neutral adviser) to negotiate proposed rule text with the agency and aims for consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency announces use of reg-neg in the Federal Register, seeks participants, uses a neutral chair/facilitator, and the process is subject to the Federal Advisory Committee Act. Negotiated rulemaking supplements APA procedures and does not replace statutory obligations; consensus usually leads to publication of the draft rule and agency commitment to issue it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) publication and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM must be published in the Federal Register unless all persons affected are named and personally served or otherwise have actual notice; it describes the proposed changes and tells the public how to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No particular format is required for written comments (from postcards to legal briefs). Courts have required at least 30 days for comment periods; E.O. 12866 suggests 60 days for most rules. If hearings are planned their time and place are often announced in the NPRM. Agencies must consider all comments and include responses to significant comments in the preamble to the final rule; comments are typically stored in a docket on Regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment rulemaking defined (including 30-day effective delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment (informal) rulemaking consists of an NPRM, a comment period, promulgation of the final rule, and a 30-day delay in the rule's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other statutes and executive orders add additional requirements to this basic APA process.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA role in regulatory review and PRA administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within OMB administers the Paperwork Reduction Act and oversees Presidential review of rules, acting as the central regulatory-review office for the White House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA Administrator is Presidentially appointed with Senate confirmation. OIRA reviews 'significant regulatory actions' per E.O. 12866; OIRA also has separate processes for free-standing ICRs and ICRs embedded in regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic statute / enabling statute requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An organic statute establishes a federal agency and often gives it specific authority to issue rules; such statutes are also called enabling or program statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency's power to issue binding regulations must derive from its organic/enabling statute; examples include the Atomic Energy Act and Federal Aviation Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) thresholds and review
rubrics_metrics.description: PRA requires agencies to obtain OIRA approval before requesting the same type of information from ten or more businesses and individuals; OIRA evaluates duplicative requests and public burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA distinguishes processes for free-standing information collection requests (e.g., tax forms) versus requests embedded in proposed regulations; agencies must estimate response costs and time in their ICRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance standards (performance-based regulation) vs prescriptive regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards state desired outcomes without prescribing how to achieve them, contrasting with prescriptive ('command-and-control') specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance standards let regulated entities choose the most efficient compliance method; regulated industries often prefer them, and agencies frequently issue guidance documents in response to requests for specifics on how to meet performance targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language / plain writing requirements and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language is communication an audience can readily understand on first reading; federal memos and the Plain Writing Act of 2010 require clear government documents (with some statutory exclusions noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles include: (1) use reader-oriented writing (write for customers); (2) use natural expression (write as you would speak, commonly used words); (3) make the document visually appealing (presentation that highlights main points). OIRA memorandum M-11-15 implements the Plain Writing Act and lists other mandates requiring clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble content and role
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble explains the reasons for regulatory action and for proposed rules contains basis for the proposal, hearings, contact persons, comment dates, and related materials; final-rule preambles include the statement of 'basis and purpose' and responses to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preambles are not part of regulatory text in the CFR and are not legally enforceable, but they form part of the informal record that courts review to determine arbitrary or capricious action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential review history and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential review of rules (via OIRA) has evolved through successive executive orders (e.g., E.O. 12291, 12866, 13563) to provide varying degrees of White House oversight, particularly of 'significant regulatory actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally applies to executive agencies and not independent regulatory agencies, though efforts (e.g., E.O. 13579 and OLC memos) have attempted to extend review to independents. OMB also reviews agency legislative proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Act disclosure and access obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Privacy Act (5 U.S.C. § 552a) requires agencies to publish the 'system of records' they maintain on individuals, to inform individuals about uses of their personal information, and to permit individuals to access and correct their records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the individual named may request copies of personal records; the Act includes procedures and exemptions similar to FOIA and there is a tension between Privacy Act protections and FOIA's disclosure goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations.gov eRulemaking portal and docketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov serves as a central portal for public comment on pending proposed rules, review of comments filed by others, and an archive for rulemaking dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally developed under the eRulemaking Program at EPA and later moved to GSA (PMO, Executive Committee, Advisory Board, workgroups); most agencies keep comments in a single docket file accessible via the website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory agency definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulatory agency is any agency delegated authority by Congress to issue regulations, licenses, set rates, or take similar actions; historically often independent commissions but increasingly executive departments and single-headed agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Today there are at least 100 regulatory agencies in the federal government; terminology overlaps with 'independent regulatory agency.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Agenda / Unified Agenda publication requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish a semi-annual Unified Agenda (regulatory agenda and regulatory flexibility agenda) listing pending regulatory actions with minimum content: regulation identification number (RIN), brief summary, legal authority, any legal deadline, and a knowledgeable contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO 12866 requires these elements; the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires listing rules likely to significantly impact small entities; the Unified Agenda is compiled by RISC and available online at RegInfo.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For rules that will affect a significant number of small entities, agencies must prepare a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (RFA) at both proposed and final stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RFA must include: (1) an estimate of the number and type of small entities affected; (2) a detailed description of recordkeeping and compliance requirements; and (3) a discussion of alternatives considered to reduce burden. SBREFA (1996) amended RFA to allow judicial challenges for non-compliance and to require agency assistance and adjusted enforcement policy for small businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective Regulatory Review requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 13563 requires agencies to periodically review significant regulations to identify rules that may be outmoded, ineffective, insufficient, or excessively burdensome and to modify, streamline, expand, or repeal them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.O. 13610 added reporting details requiring agencies to submit draft retrospective-review reports to OIRA on the second Monday of January and July each year; this implements a 'look back' system for existing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROCIS system functions and public transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: ROCIS (RISC/OIRA Consolidated Information System) manages regulatory agenda, regulatory review, and information collection review data for RISC and OIRA and supports agency submissions to the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ROCIS supports OIRA's workflow, houses historical and current regulatory data, and most information submitted through ROCIS is available to the public on RegInfo.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule definition and publication requirement under APA
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'rule' under the APA is any agency statement of future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy, or to describe the agency’s organization, procedure, or practice requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To have the force of law, a rule must be issued under delegated congressional authority and follow appropriate rulemaking requirements; agencies’ organizational descriptions and rules of general applicability must be published in the Federal Register, and many rules must be proposed first unless an exception applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment docketing and agency obligation to consider comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider all comments received in response to an NPRM before issuing a final rule and must include responses to significant comments in the final-rule preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most comments are filed electronically (agency website or Regulations.gov) and are maintained in a single docket file; the agency's consideration of comments is part of the informal record reviewed by courts for arbitrary-or-capricious claims.
